But Painted Desert is nothing of the sort. Instead, we have one of the missing links in the evolution of ambient country, an astonishing melding of skeletal machine rhythms and big sky guitars. Read More Close Horse Lords :: Demand to Be Taken to Heaven Alive! Horse Lords return with what may well be their strangest and prettiest album yet. Here the Baltimore-Berlin quartet adds Protestant hymn-singing, swamp boogie, early computer music and even robot funk to their signature brand of phase-shifting krautrock groove. It is an alluring, compelling mix that plays with themes of religious devotion and utopian longing. Fifteen years into their career, Horse Lords are still making some of the most radical, captivating music of our time. The natural extension of Happy End with a bit more of a singer-songwriter orientation, Kosaka pieces together what could be the finest example of American country rock through the lens of a Japanese perfectionism. Don’t let that fool you. The tunes are loose. They linger like a haze of humidity long after the sun has departed beneath the western horizon. Working from updated Treasure Isle and Studio One riddims, Thompson transforms each track into its own sonic chamber of mystery, where thunder, synths, cuckoo clocks, telephones, and doorbells point toward the future of dub while remaining deeply rooted in its past. As the days flatten into heat haze and evenings linger just a little longer, familiar records reveal unexpected contours. As August stretches on, the Aquarium Drunkard crew returns with another installment of our annual Dog Days roundup: a stack of old favorites, forgotten treasures, new discoveries, and seasonal obsessions. Twenty Years Inside The Eraser Posted on August 3, 2026 August 3, 2026 Listening with the hindsight of twenty years, The Eraser has lost none of its curved-glass cut and glimmer. Yorke was still riding high on a generational songwriting run and, with Nigel Godrich’s help, what obstacles remained between idea and execution had been removed. Big Black :: Two Moonlins And Mother Posted on July 30, 2026 July 29, 2026 Before Pharoah Sanders, before Blazing Saddles, before Muhammad Ali’s training camp, there was “Two Moonlins And Mother.” Big Black’s compact boogaloo gem distills a lifetime of rhythm into three minutes of humid, percussive heat. The Aquarium Drunkard Show: SIRIUS/XMU (7pm PDT, Channel 35) Posted on July 29, 2026 July 27, 2026 Broadcasting from northeast Los Angeles — the Aquarium Drunkard Show on SIRIUS/XMU, channel 35. 7pm California time, Wednesdays. Slow dissolve. Kosmische drift. ECM-adjacent. Synth meditations. Folk reveries. Keith Jarrett. Harmonia. Eno. Ashra. Gaussian Curve. Chet Baker. Sybille Baier. CAN. Fellow travelers. 34.1090° N, 118.2334° W Vin Gordon with Lee Perry and The Upsetters :: Musical Bones Posted on July 29, 2026 July 29, 2026 Recorded at the height of the Black Ark with Lee “Scratch” Perry at the controls and The Upsetters firing on all cylinders, Musical Bones gave legendary trombonist Vin Gordon the rare opportunity to step out of the backline and into the spotlight. Originally released in 1975 as a UK white-label pressing of just 300 copies, it vanished almost as quickly as it appeared, becoming one of reggae’s great collector’s grails. Charlie Hunter Quartet :: Natty Dread Posted on July 29, 2026 July 28, 2026 The Charlie Hunter Quartet’s track-by-track cover of Bob Marley’s 1974 classic Natty Dread probably shouldn’t work, but somehow the sublimely talented soul jazz guitarist and his group pull it off. Rather than staying faithful to the sound of Marley’s reggae standard, Hunter captures the joy and exuberance of the music. Mixing in salsa, jazz-funk, high-life and blues, Hunter’s quartet turn what might have been a polite tribute into an explosive celebration. It should be on every summer playlist. Transmissions :: Erin Osmon Posted on July 29, 2026 July 29, 2026 This week on the show, we welcome Nashville-based music journalist, critic and author Erin Osmon, to discuss her tremendous book, W⁠on’t Back Down: Heartland Rock and the Fight for America ⁠, which chronicles how heartland rock, typified by artists like Bruce Springsteen, John Mellencamp, Tom Petty, Bob Seger, and more, brought a populist, Americana-inspired sound to the airwaves of the radio and MTV. The Visitors :: My Good Friends Posted on July 28, 2026 July 28, 2026 Issued in 1977, My Good Friends captures a moment when eastern Nigeria’s musicians folded highlife, funk, soul, and psychedelia into something restless and idiosyncratic. The results are gloriously untidy. While the contemporary story of Nigerian popular music is often told through towering figures like Fela Kuti, William Onyeabor, and King Sunny Adé, records like this reveal a parallel current—one built on synthesis rather than singularity. The Box Set: An Appreciation, Vol. 3 Posted on July 28, 2026 July 28, 2026 The initial standard for a compact disc was 74 minutes. Legend has it the length was decided upon in order to fit all of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony onto a single disc. In terms of format, the arrival and adoption of the CD in 1983 changed not only how we listen to recorded music, but how it’s presented as an art form. No longer beholden to the 22 minute confines of a “12 side, artists began experimenting with the medium… as did labels. Welcome to the third installment of The Box Set: An Appreciation. Echo Upstairs :: Estranhos Lugares Para os Olhos Posted on July 27, 2026 July 27, 2026 For years, Brazilian shoegaze has felt like a borrowed climate. Estranhos Lugares Para os Olhos suggests otherwise, recasting the genre’s familiar wall of sound in tropical hues. Echo Upstairs doesn’t abandon shoegaze’s dream-state—it changes the weather. Choose Life: The Trainspotting Soundtrack at 30 Posted on July 27, 2026 July 25, 2026 Thirty years on, the Trainspotting soundtrack remains one of the defining musical documents of the 1990s. Equal parts mixtape, time capsule, and gateway drug, it introduced a generation to Iggy Pop, Underworld, Lou Reed, and a world of records just beyond the mainstream.
